title: 101 Zen Stories, Part 2: Japanese Zen Stories
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The main teaching of the Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of humility, patience, and directness in spiritual practice. Through stories from Zen history, such as Ryōnen's self-mutilation, Bankei's humble response to a priest's boastfulness, and others like "Midnight Excursion" and "A Drop of Water," the teacher illustrates that true awakening comes not through punishment or harshness, but rather through kindness, understanding, and attention to detail. By embracing this approach, we can cultivate a deeper understanding of ourselves and the world around us, and find our own path towards spiritual growth and awakening.

It's all on the website.
All right.

So let's finish my coda to the 50 talks with a few more.
Last one, I promise.
Zen stories, a selection from the second half of Nyogen Senzaki's early collection of Japanese Zen stories.
*101 Zen Stories* was the title of the book, one of the very first books in English talking about the Zen spirit.
Of course, it talks about it in a certain kind of language from that time, and from a Japanese speaker writing in English.
So we have definitely changed the way we express things.
But I think it's been really interesting to hear a little bit about these old stories.
Some of them are standard stories that get quoted here and there in Dharma talks.
So it's kind of fun to hear them in the original, if there is such a thing as an original version of a family story, right?
They change as they go.

The other thing that's really neat, among the many things I love about Nyogen Senzaki, besides his incredible chutzpah in staying behind in America with almost no English, in his mid, maybe mid-20s or something, completely alone in a new culture because he wanted to introduce Zen here, is that he couldn't really stay in touch with his teacher, which would be the usual thing.
He was pretty young to leave his teacher.
He'd usually do a much longer apprenticeship in that Japanese Zen system that he was a part of.
He was kind of adopted into it.
He was an orphan, kind of sucked into the temple world as a young monk.
So he couldn't really stay in touch with his teacher, Shaku Soen, Soen Shaku, also a famous figure in this early period.
They exchanged a few letters that we know of, and maybe a few more that have been lost.
He knew that his teacher was still alive until his teacher died and he got word.
But every evening, I just remembered this, he would go and face himself towards the Pacific Ocean.
He was in San Francisco, then he was in LA.
Every evening he would face east, or face west, sorry, face west.
We call it the east, but actually we go west to get there.
And he would do three prostrations, holding his teacher in his heart.
It's a beautiful thing to think about.
That was his way of feeling connected to his teacher as he learned English and hung out his plank after 17 years of preparation, and started running a little sangha in LA in his apartment.

He was trying to figure out how to talk about this stuff in English and how to do some version of the monastic practice he had received, in a new land where people didn't know about all this Japanese stuff at all.
Anyway, one of the things he did early on, before he started the sangha work, before he was ready to do any of that, was put this little book out.
I still haven't been able to find out whether it got any kind of circulation, or whether it was a tiny, back-of-the-bookstore press somewhere in LA or something like that.
So who knows who ever actually saw this book.
But eventually Paul Reps, as I mentioned last week, who published the important book in the 50s, *Zen Flesh, Zen Bones*, kind of sucked this book into his book, and that book was pretty well known.
It was published by a major publisher.
He was connected to an important publisher, part of a literary circle in America.
Paul Reps was, not Nyogen Senzaki.
Okay, more than enough intro.
Story 53.
No, sorry, Story 50.
Ryōnen's Clear Realization.
Get organized here, okay.
*The Buddhist nun, known as Ryōnen, was born in 1797.
She was a granddaughter of the famous Japanese warrior, Shigen.
Her poetical genius and alluring beauty were such that at 17 she was serving the empress as one of the ladies of the court.
Even at such a youthful age, fame awaited her.
The beloved empress died suddenly, and Ryōnen's hopeful dreams vanished.
She suddenly was acutely aware of the impermanence of life in the world, and she desired just from then on to study Zen.
Her relatives disagreed, however, and practically forced her into a marriage.
With a promise that she might become a nun after she'd born three children, Ryōnen assented.
Before she was 25, she'd accomplished this condition.*
You know, had the three kids.
*Then her husband and relatives could no longer dissuade her from her desire.
So she shaved her head, took the name of Ryōnen, which means to realize clearly, and started a pilgrimage.
She came to the city of Edo and asked Tetsugya to accept her as a disciple.
She's been a teacher.
At one glance, the master rejected her because she was too beautiful.
Ryōnen went to another master, Hakuo, and Hakuo refused her for the same reason, saying that her beauty would only make trouble in the monastery.
So Ryōnen obtained a hot iron, placed it against her face.
In a few moments, her beauty had vanished forever, and Hakuo accepted her as a disciple.*
*Commemorating this occasion, Ryōnen wrote a poem on the back of a little mirror.*
The back of a mirror.
*In the service of my empress, I burned incense to perfume my exquisite clothes.
Now, as a homeless mendicant, I burn my face to enter a Zen temple.*
Yeah.
*Later, when Ryōnen was about to pass from this world, she wrote another poem. 66 times have these eyes beheld the changing scene of autumn.
I have said enough about moonlight.
Ask no more.
Only listen to the voices of pines and cedars when no wind stirs.*
66 times is her death poem.
*66 times have these eyes beheld the changing scene of autumn.
I have said enough about moonlight.
Ask no more.
Only listen to the voice of pines and cedars when no wind stirs.*
So that's pretty powerful.
A mix of really challenging things there, right?
Our horror, learning about yet another woman who had to disfigure herself in order to follow her heart.
But you've got to have some admiration too, right, for that level of dedication, that courage, that willingness, and maybe all kinds of other feelings.
Who knows what really happened and how this story came to us through the misogynist centuries, but it's a powerful story.
Another thing that's in there is kind of deep in the tradition, and it's a little bit of a creepy part of our tradition.
I like to mention once in a while the things that aren't so lovely, or are challenging anyway, about what we're doing these days, or that came before us.
One is that harming your body, doing something to your body, is a really old tradition in Asian Buddhism to show your sincerity, and it persists into the common era.
I know of one case, secondhand.
I've never met this person, but I know someone who knew her.

The Japanese Zen sewing teacher, I think her name was Josu-san, came over to San Francisco in the 60s sometime to help Suzuki Roshi and his students learn how to do the Zen sewing that we now somehow know how to do up here.
It's amazing we can do this now.
Hand sewing the rakusu that you receive with Jukai, with receiving the precepts, hand sewing the okesa, this bigger garment that we receive when we do priest ordinations, and other bits and pieces.
It's a powerful practice to put our hands to work in this way, each stitch like a mantra, like a prayer, and a lot comes up for people doing this practice.
So it's a real great thing that we have received that tradition.
Anyway, Josu-san trained Blanche Hartman, who was an abbot of San Francisco Zen Center, one of my teachers.
Blanche actually came up here.
She was one of the first, or maybe the second, I can't remember, person from San Francisco Zen Center, besides Norman, to come up here, early 2000s maybe, and help us sew rakusu.
Blanche remembered that Josu-san was missing the tip of one of her pinkies.
The reason why is that at one point in her career as a nun, she wanted to change teachers.
I don't remember why, I have this written down somewhere, I couldn't find it.
But her teacher refused to let her go, there's much of a feeling of control in that system.
So she put her finger in a candle all night, until the tip of her finger was cauterized away.
Can you imagine that?
This was not uncommon, though, not uncommon.
And then her teacher agreed.
Isn't that powerful, to think about that action?
Horrifying as it sounds to me now, and maybe I don't know how it sounds to you, that somehow helped us have Zen sewing in Bellingham, Washington in 2020.
It goes way back.
You don't need to do that now.
But there's some depth to this tradition, and some levels of commitment that are hard for us to quite get our minds around.

We could have all kinds of judgments about the culture in which that was okay, or that was respected, especially, and I don't know if this happened more often with female or male monastics, I really don't know.
But here it is, in *101 Zen Stories*.
Burning the face, burning the finger.
Story 53.
The giver should be thankful.
*When Setsu was the master of Engaku in Kamakura, he required larger quarters, so he needed to expand the temple, since those he was teaching in were overcrowded.
So Umesasebe, a merchant of Edo, decided to donate 500 pieces of gold, called five ryo, towards the construction of a more commodious temple.
So he brought [unclear: "the mine"] to the teacher.
Setsu, the teacher said, alright, I'll take it.
And so Umesu, the merchant, gave Setsu the sack of gold.
But he was dissatisfied with the attitude of this teacher.
One might live a whole year on three ryo.
And here the merchant had not even been thanked for 500,* oh sorry, I had it wrong, *500 ryo,* huge amount of money.
*So the merchant said, in that sack are 500 ryo.
You told me that before, replied Setsu.
Even if I am a wealthy merchant, 500 ryo is a lot of money, said Umesu.
Do you want me to thank you for it? asked Setsu.
You ought to, replied Umesa.
Why should I? inquired Setsu.
It's the giver who should be thankful.*

So there are many, many stories like this in the Japanese Zen tradition of hard-ass, uncompromising Zen teachers who are willing to give up the huge donation or give up their lives to make a teaching point.
Reading these again, I realized that I've heard these stories a lot more about Japanese teachers than Chinese teachers.
For me this is more of a Japanese thing, to be this stern, uncompromising figure, pure in some way, demonstrating purity.
So I won't manage our donors that way if we get around to trying to raise money for a building.
I'll say thank you, just in case you're wondering.
Maybe I'll read the story though, but it could have been different if you were in ancient Japan: "Yeah, whatever, it's a million dollars, what do I care?
You should be thankful to give it to us."
Next, the true path.
*The True Path.
Just before Ninakawa passed away, Zen Master Ikkyu visited him.
"Shall I lead you on?"
Ikkyu asked.
Ninakawa replied, "I came here alone, I now go alone.
What help could you be to me?"*
*Ikkyu, the teacher, answered, "Do you think you really come and go?
That is your delusion.
Let me show you the path in which there is no coming and no going."
With these words, Ikkyu had revealed the path so clearly that Ninakawa, who was dying, smiled, relaxed, and passed away.*
So many of these stories, and so much of what we're really about, is about this reality, right?
We're here, right?
It's always kind of behind us somewhere.
We don't think about it.
About death, right?
Birth and death.
So I'll be sure and give your best tomorrow.
I'm going to go visit our member, Anne Mikkelsen.
She was far in the process of living with brain cancer and soon will be dying.
And I don't know if telling her there's no coming and no going will help, but Edie is going to come too, and we'll try to embody that teaching, that it's okay, it's okay.
I talked to Anne's son, and it sounds like she is pretty peaceful.
Sleeping a lot, facing things okay, but I'll report back later on how she is.
I'll ask her what I can share.
So we're seeing some life and death in our own sangha lately, aren't we?
And we won't start seeing less of it.
So how do we understand the nature of living and dying, of being and no longer being?
Are we this temporary little fragile creature that is excited to be alive until we're not, and then we're miserable, when we're going to lose everything, lose our life?
Or are we in some way some embodiment of life itself?
More like a wave on the ocean.
I love that metaphor, I hope I don't abuse it too much, to see ourselves not as this individual person, but part of this larger dance of life and death.
It doesn't mean that death isn't sad.
I hope that all of us who know and appreciate Anne will cry at her passing when that happens, and I'm sure her kids will be sad, and people who know her and love her.
But in a certain way it's not so sad, right?
It's so natural, right?
It's like the sunset, you know?
The sunset is beautiful.
We're not exactly sad that the sun is falling below the horizon, because we have trust, we have faith that it's part of a bigger thing.
Dawn is coming.
So lots of stories in here about birth and death.
Story 57, The Gates of Paradise.
*Gates of Paradise.
A soldier named Noboshige came to Hakuin and said, "Is there really a paradise and a hell?"
"Who are you?" inquired Hakuin, the teacher.
"I am a samurai," the warrior replied.
"You, a soldier?" exclaimed Hakuin.
"What kind of ruler would have you as his guard?
Your face looks like a beggar's."*
*And Noboshige, the samurai, became so angry he began to draw his sword.
And Hakuin continued, "So you have a sword?
Your weapon is probably much too dull to cut off my head."
As Noboshige drew his sword, Hakuin remarked, "Here, here is hell."
And at these words the samurai, perceiving the master's discipline, sheathed his sword and bowed.*
*"Here, here is heaven.
Here is paradise," said Hakuin.*
Classic story.
And again, the teacher willing to put it all on the line.
His very head on the line to make a point.
I like some of the modern psychology studies where they kind of trick the subjects and tell them the study is about something else, to see how they actually behave.
So these are a little bit like this.
Early psychology.
Tricking this samurai into anger.
Showing him the hell of anger and violence to get his way.
And it's experiential, right?
So our practice is very experiential.
Kind of a cute fable in a way, but also a powerful story.
Story 71, Learning to be Silent.
*Learning to be Silent.
The pupils of the Tendai school used to study meditation before Zen entered Japan.
Four of them were such intimate friends that they promised one another that they would now observe seven days of silence so they could meditate.
On the first day, all were silent.
Their meditation had begun auspiciously.
But when night came and the oil lamps were growing dim, one of the pupils could not help exclaiming to a servant.*
*And the second pupil was so surprised to hear the first one talk.
"We're not supposed to say a word," he said.
And then the third one said, "You two are so stupid, why are you talking?"
And the fourth one said, "I am the only one that hasn't talked."*
So if you've had trouble keeping silence at sesshin, it turns out to be a very old problem.
Even before Zen got to Japan, people were struggling with keeping silence during sesshin.
Here's a little more on donor management.
*The Blockhead Lord.
Two Zen teachers, Daigu and Godo, were invited to visit the Lord.
Upon arriving, Godo said to the Lord, "You are wise by nature and have an inborn ability to learn Zen."
The other teacher, Daigu, said, "Nonsense!
Why do you flatter this Blockhead?
He may be a Lord, but he doesn't know a thing about Zen."*
*And so, instead of building a temple for Godo, the one who flattered him, the Lord built it for Daigu, the one who challenged him, and studied Zen with him.*
So, a little more donor management advice for us when we call people up about the capital campaign.
Don't flatter them, you know.
Don't flatter them.
Maybe don't tell them they don't know nothing and that they're Blockheads, though.
Maybe we should skip that part.
Let's see.
Story 80, The Real Miracle.
*The Real Miracle.

When Bankei was preaching at Ryomon Temple, a Shinshu priest, who believed in salvation through the repetition of the name of the Buddha of Love, Amida Buddha, was jealous of Bankei's large audience and wanted to debate with him.
Bankei was in the middle of a talk when the priest appeared, but the fellow made such a disturbance that Bankei stopped his dharma talk and asked about the noise.
"The founder of our sect!" boasted the Shinshu priest from the back.
"He had such miraculous powers that he held a brush in his hand on one bank of a river, and his attendant held a piece of paper up at the other bank.
The teacher wrote the holy name of Amida through the air.
Can you do such a wonderful thing?"
Bankei replied lightly, "Perhaps your fox can perform that trick, but that's not the manner of Zen.
My miracle is, when I feel hungry, I eat.
When I feel thirsty, I drink."*
So we met Bankei in the last talk.
He was a famously popular teacher, and when he gave talks, he gave really accessible talks.
He did them in marketplace buildings and stuff like that, outside of the monastery.
He was a popularizer of Zen.
Anyway, other people get jealous, and there's a couple of different stories about rival priests showing up.
There were huge talks, and he pissed off [unclear: "pissed off"] some people.

But here also, the wonderful Zen teaching, something we really can't practice very deeply in the Rohatsu sesshin we were talking about before, that it really is a miracle to be alive, to notice, to feel, to respond.
When tired, sleep.
When hungry, eat.
When thirsty, drink.
That immediacy and that directness.
When someone's cold, give a blanket.
When someone's upset, offer comfort.
Just right there, right there.
So that's the miracle we need.
Story 82, Nothing Exists.
*Nothing Exists.
Yamaoka Tesshu, a young student of Zen, visited one master after another.
Then he called upon Dokuan of Shokoku.
Desiring to show his attainment, the young student said, "The mind, Buddha, sentient beings, after all, do not exist.
The true nature of all phenomena is emptiness.
There is no realization, no delusion, no sage, no mediocrity.
There is no giving and nothing to be received."
Dokuan, the teacher, who was smoking quietly, said nothing.
And suddenly he whacked Yamaoka with his bamboo pipe, which made the youth jump in anger.
"If nothing exists," required Dokuan, "where did this anger come from?"*
So, more play here.
And there's a lot of humor in these stories, of course.
And Zen training is also dynamic and playful.
And who knows if the hitting each other was mock hitting or real hitting, maybe some of both.
But the other piece here is that the monk was not incorrect.
So it's kind of a trope in Zen to be giving us all these teachings, you know what I mean?
Zen respects all the other Mahayana teachings and the early teachings, and they're all in here.
We just chanted the Heart Sutra, which said more or less exactly what this young student said.

And Zen is also famous for putting in the words of the founder this famous verse, supposedly Bodhidharma said, but probably it's later teachers who said he said, that what Zen is really about is this:
*A special transmission outside the scriptures, not depending on words and letters, directly pointing to the mind, seeing into one's true nature, attaining Buddhahood.
A special transmission outside the scriptures, not depending on words and letters, directly pointing to the mind, seeing into one's true nature, attaining Buddhahood.*
So there's this beautiful kind of thread there, you know, immediacy, right?
Directness like the previous story.
And yet, part of how we get there is study.
Part of how we get there is teachings.
But the invitation is to inhabit them deeply and not show off.
You might get a whack.
I don't know how to do the Zen whack through Zoom.
They didn't have that problem.
There's the Zen shout.
I suppose I can do that.
Let's do just a couple more and then a few minutes to just chat together about Zen stories again.
Midnight Excursion.
*Midnight Excursion.
Many students were studying meditation under the Zen Master Sengai.
But one of them used to arise at night, climb out over the temple wall and go to town on a pleasure jaunt.
Sengai, inspecting the dormitory one night, found that this student was missing and also discovered the high stool he had used to scale the wall.
So Sengai removed the stool and stood there in its place.
Stood there all night.*
*When the wanderer returned, not knowing that Sengai was the stool now, he put his feet on the Master's head and jumped down into the grounds.
Discovering what he had done, he was aghast.
Sengai said, "It's very chilly in the early morning.
Do be careful not to catch cold."
And that pupil never went out again.*
Those are some of my favorite stories.
There's a lot of these too, where the teacher teaches not by hitting, you know, not by being harsh, but by patience, by kindness, by showing up.
It may be a little embarrassment, you know, the power of embarrassment.
And this was a monastic situation where everyone was expected to follow this very intense schedule and never leave the monastery.
So you're not supposed to sneak out and go drinking.
So he didn't chew him out, right?
Just welcomed him back and made a little suggestion.
Like, I see you, basically.
I see you.
Straighten the kid out, you know.
Two more.
A Drop of Water.
*A Drop of Water.
A Zen Master named Gisan asked a young student to bring him a pail of water to cool his bath.
The student brought the water and, after cooling the bath, threw on the ground the little water in the bucket that was left over.
"Idiot!" the Master scolded him.
"Why didn't you give the rest of the water to the plants?
What right have you to waste even one drop of water in this temple?"
The young student attained Zen in that instant.*
Woke up.
And he changed his name to Tekisui. [unclear: "Tekkisui"].
Which means drop of water.
So there was a little shouting there, but, you know, strategic.
And this powerful lesson, right?
Pay attention.
Even one drop.
Even one grain of rice, right?
Even, you know, burning one less gallon of gas in our daily routine.
That the world and all life is a treasure, you know, to respect it all.
Down to the drop.
And humility, right?
The student naming himself after this lesson where he was in the wrong, you know.
He was in the wrong, but it helped him wake up to this truth.
Last one for now.
The Silent Temple.
*The Silent Temple.
Shuichi was a one-eyed teacher of Zen.
Sparkling with enlightenment, he taught his disciples in Tokufu Temple.
But his teaching was a quiet teaching.
Day and night the whole temple stood in silence.
No sound at all.
Even the reciting of sutras was abolished by the teacher.
His pupils had nothing to do but meditate.
And when the old master passed away, a neighbor heard the ringing of bells and the recitation of sutras.
And she knew Shuichi had gone.*
That's beautiful.
I'm going to read that one again.
*Shuichi was a one-eyed teacher of Zen.
Sparkling with enlightenment, he taught his disciples in Tokufu Temple.
But his teaching was a quiet one.
Day and night the whole temple stood in silence with no sound at all.
Even the reciting of sutras was abolished by the teacher.
And the students had nothing to do but meditate.
When the master passed away, an old neighbor heard the ringing of the bells and heard the recitation of sutras.
And she knew that Shuichi had gone.*
So, a few more Zen stories for us.

Another thing that's kind of fun is there are a few little collections of modern Zen stories, including some modern stories in the wonderful Hidden Lamp collection that Florence Caplow and Susan Moon put together, stories of women teachers.
And a few of the stories that they included are in this book from way back when, by Nyogen Senzaki.
Any thoughts about those stories or stories in general?
Are there things that you learned in your life through story?
What are your thoughts about stories?
And to say Zen stories is extra, not just stories.
Oh, you really liked that last story, didn't you?
Beautiful.
Thank you.
I'm actually serious.
I don't need anybody to say anything.
But pay attention to that.
I think we don't always notice the stories.
We think we're all rational and step by step and sensible.
But I think our minds work more in story and myth and legend than we realize.
That we're actually a little more mythological in our daily lives than we quite realize.
And the things we enact have implanted many things that we feel and believe and respond to in certain ways, but it got planted there through story.
The story of me is the biggest story of all.
Me and who I think I am.
Anything else?
Anything coming up?
I'll give a few minutes, but I don't need to milk the cow or anything like that.
*Our intentions equally extend to every being and place, with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
